title: The fifth hole
translation: "Ryūaki, who plays the mouth organ, is someone who really counts in music. The other day he came and told me: 'It's probably a foolish thought, and very forward of me, but I've been quietly wondering if there isn't something a little off about the fifth hole on the flute.

'Here's why. Between each pair of neighbouring holes, one note of the scale is left out, all the way along the flute. Only the fifth hole has no note left out between it and the next one, and yet it sits the same distance away as all the others. So it sounds wrong. When you play that hole, you always have to pull your mouth back a little. If you can't pull back far enough, it's out of tune with everything else. Very few people can play it properly.'
That's a remarkable piece of thinking, and really interesting. It's what people mean when they say the old masters fear the ones who come after them."

Another day, Kagemochi, who plays the flute, told me: "The mouth organ is tuned completely before you play, so all you do is blow. The flute you tune as you go, with your breath. Each hole needs what your teacher passed on to you, plus your own feel for it, and you have to put your heart into it. That isn't only true of the fifth. You can't simply say 'always pull back'. Play badly, and no hole sounds good. A good player makes every one of them fit. If the notes don't match, that's the player's fault, not the instrument's."

literal: The Shijō middle counsellor said: 'Ryūaki is a person of distinction in (his) art.
The other day he came and said: "It is the height of shallow thinking and extremely rude, but I privately think that there may be something slightly questionable about the fifth hole of the flute.
The reason is that the kan hole is hyōjō and the fifth hole is shimomu.
The jō hole is sōjō; next, leaving out fushō, the shaku hole is ōshiki.
Next, leaving out rankei, the chū hole is banshiki; between chū and roku there is shinsen.
In this way, in between, each (pair) steals one pitch, but only the fifth hole has no pitch between it and jō, and yet the spacing is equal, so its sound is unpleasant.
So when one blows this hole, one always pulls back.
When one cannot pull back fully, it does not match things.
People who can play it are rare", he said.
The height of reasoning: truly interesting.
What they call "the predecessor fears the later-born" is this', so it was.
On another day, what Kagemochi said was: 'The shō, since one holds it fully tuned, one simply blows.

The flute, since it is a thing one tunes as one goes, within the breath, while blowing, putting one's heart into each hole, adding one's natural knack on top of the oral teaching, is not limited to the fifth hole.
One should not decide simply that one pulls back.
If one blows badly, no hole is pleasant.
A master makes every one of them fit.
That the tuning does not match things is the person's fault, not the instrument's flaw', he said.

notes.text: Shijō Takasuke (1292–1352), a courtier of Emperor Go-Daigo; {黄門|くわうもん} is the Chinese name for his post, middle counsellor (the 1925 edition's identification; some modern commentaries suggest Shijō Takakage instead). {命|めい}ぜられて{曰|いは}く: a very respectful 'he said'.

Toyohara no Ryūaki, a court musician and a master of the {笙|しやう}, the mouth organ (the 1925 edition's gloss). The Toyohara family were hereditary players of that instrument. So the man finding fault with the flute is not a flute player.

notes.quote: 短慮の至り、極めて荒涼の事なれども
notes.text: Polite self-deprecation before a criticism: 'the height of shallow thinking' (the 1925 edition: a humble phrase) and {荒涼|くわうりやう} 'outrageously rude'.

{横笛|わうてき}: the transverse flute of court music (today usually called {龍笛|りゆうてき}), with seven finger holes. The holes have names: {六|ろく}, {中|ちゆう}, {夕|さく}, {上|じやう}, {五|ご}, {干|かん} and one more. The 1925 edition places the fifth hole third from the end of the flute.

The names are those of the twelve pitches of court music, about one per semitone: {平調|ひやうでう}, {勝絶|しようぜつ}, {下無|しもむ}, {双調|さうでう}, {鳧鐘|ふしよう}, {黄鐘|わうしき}, {鸞鏡|らんけい}, {盤渉|ばんしき}, {神仙|しんせん}, in rising order. Ryūaki's map of the flute: kan hyōjō, (shōzetsu skipped), five shimomu, jō sōjō, (fushō skipped), shaku ōshiki, (rankei skipped), chū banshiki, (shinsen between chū and roku). The translation keeps only the pattern.
'Steals one pitch': between neighbouring holes, one pitch is skipped. Between the fifth hole and jō nothing is skipped, so these two should sit closer together than the others. They don't.
のく: 'to pull back, to move away'. Commentaries explain it as moving the mouth slightly away from the mouth hole; the exact technique is not certain. のけあへぬ: 'cannot pull back enough'.
{料簡|れうけん}: 'reasoning, considered judgement'. Modern りょうけん means 'intention, attitude', as in {了見|りようけん}が{狭|せま}い 'narrow-minded'.

An echo of the Analects: {後生|こうせい}{畏|おそ}るべし, 'the young are to be feared', because they may surpass you. The text does not spell out who the {先達|せんだち} ('those who went before') and the {後生|こうせい} are here.
Ōga no Kagemochi (the 1925 edition gives the family name). The Ōga were the hereditary flute players at court, so this is the specialist's answer.

notes.quote: 笙は調べおほせてもちたれば
notes.text: The {笙|しやう} is a mouth organ of seventeen bamboo pipes, each with its own fixed note. Once tuned, it plays in tune. A flute's pitch depends on how you blow.

notes.quote: 口伝の上に、性骨を加へて
notes.text: {口伝|くでん}: teaching passed on by word of mouth, from master to student. {性骨|せいこつ}: an inborn knack (the 1925 edition: the 骨 one is born with; compare the {骨|こつ} of section 150).
{呂律|りよりつ}: tuning, the scales of court music (the 1925 edition: pitch). Modern ろれつ, as in ろれつが{回|まは}らない 'to slur your words', comes from this word.
